summary:
Archana Kamath (VP of engineering, inference engine and AI infrastructure at DigitalOcean) frames the talk around why the 'one model for everything' habit is breaking: exploding inference spend (Walmart, Uber, Microsoft are capping usage), poor cost-fit when frontier models handle trivial work, and the operational risk of depending on a single model with no failover. Her central claim is that no public leaderboard can encode the right model for a request because fit depends on the task, the surrounding system prompt and tools, acceptable cost, required latency, and end-user preference.

Tyler Gillam then presents DigitalOcean's open-source inference router, a two-part stack: an open proxy plus a purpose-built mixture-of-experts routing model. Users express preferences in natural language or decision-tree rules (cost, latency, quality, hard rules); the router honors them per request, deciding in under 200 ms with no extra cost. He demos cloud-console configuration including presets, per-task model pools, manual ranking with failover, and a 'fastest in last 30 minutes' selection policy. A side-by-side playground and a two-terminal open-code demo (build a spinning-wheel app) show the router matching prompts to smaller, cheaper models, producing comparable output for 8 cents versus 25 cents for Opus on the first session and 14 cents versus 44 cents after additional prompts. An evaluation scores the router at 90% correctness versus 95% for Opus, with significantly fewer tokens and lower latency, described as within judge margin of error.

Archana closes by reiterating the under-200 ms decision time, the purpose-built MoE routing model (open sourced via Plano), zero application code changes, free inclusion, and the claim that routing is a foundation layer beneath evaluation, caching, and personalization in a continuous improvement loop. Her takeaway: benchmarks tell part of the story, preferences tell the rest, and DigitalOcean's router exists to honor preferences without vendor lock-in.

sections.title: Why the one model habit is breaking
sections.summary: Archana Kamath introduces DigitalOcean's AI-native cloud stack, frames routing as part of the inference engine, and argues that cost, fit, and single-model risk are breaking the habit of using one model for everything. She also claims cloud-style inference cost optimization is arriving in months, not the 15 years cloud cost optimization took.

sections.title: There is no single best model
sections.summary: Archana argues the right model depends on the task, giving examples ranging from a small open model for classification to a frontier model for security-critical code review. She lists task, system prompts/tools, cost, latency, and end-user preference as dimensions no public leaderboard encodes, then hands off to Tyler Gillam.

sections.title: A router you can customize and evaluate
sections.summary: Tyler describes the open-source proxy plus a purpose-built MoE routing model. Users express preferences in natural language or decision-tree rules; the router decides per request in under 200 ms with no extra cost, claims to beat frontier models at the routing task itself, and is open source with no vendor lock-in.

sections.title: Configuring tasks, model pools and failover
sections.summary: In the cloud console, Tyler shows router presets (software engineering, general writing, knowledge bases, document intelligence) and a customized software-engineering router with per-task model pools. He demonstrates manual ranking (prefer GLM 5.2, fail over to GPT 5.2) and a 'fastest in last 30 minutes' selection policy for bug fixing.

sections.title: Side by side in the playground
sections.summary: Tyler runs three prompts side by side: single Opus vs the software-engineering router. The router matches Fibonacci to a small Maverick model, optimization to GPT 5.2, and unit tests to Claude 5 Sonnet, and is faster and cheaper each time while still framed as a 'vibe check'.

sections.title: Proving it with an evaluation
sections.summary: Tyler presents an evaluation scoring the router at 90% correctness versus Opus at 95%, described as within judge margin of error. The router uses significantly fewer tokens and is significantly faster than Opus.

sections.title: Two coding agents, and the session cost gap
sections.summary: Tyler runs the same 'build me a spinning wheel app' prompt in two open-code terminals: Opus-only on the left, router on the right, with live token and cost observability. The router matches code generation to GLM 5.2, finishes at a similar time with comparable output, and spends 8 cents versus 25 cents for Opus. After adding 'write unit tests' (matched to Claude 5 Sonnet) and 'write a readme', total session cost is 14 cents for the router versus 44 cents for Opus, and Tyler notes the gap widens as you scale.

sections.title: Routing as a foundation, with eval, caching and personalization on top
sections.summary: Archana returns to recap the live demo with quick facts: routing decision under 200 ms, purpose-built MoE model, zero application code changes, free and included, and the routing model open sourced via Plano. She frames routing as a foundation layer beneath three things built on top — eval to prove the right model works for your use case, caching to stop paying twice for the same answer, and personalization so the router learns what works for your team over time — describing this as a continuous improvement loop. She closes by restating that there is no single best model, benchmarks only tell part of the story, and DigitalOcean's router exists to honor user preferences without vendor lock-in.
